title: Logging library — severity, throttling, aggregation, then production

aiGuide.intro: The freshest reported AI-round question (5 reports, Aug–Sep 2026). Four phases, then production. Lesson 11.2 of the video course runs this exact question.
plan: Ask: what makes two logs identical? is the minimum itself written? can I inject the clock?
AI fills in Log → read its assumptions → run
Throttle + summary: you add the window table and lock rule; AI edits; run
AI writes adversarial tests with reasons; you check every expected value
Threads: decide under the lock, write outside it; AI writes the stress test
Production: bounded channel, drop and count; your three-numbers test

stages.name: Severity filtering
stages.yours: Write the class shape: minimum severity, an injected `IClock`, an array of sinks. One comment per rule: the exact format `"{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"`, and that a failing sink must not stop the others. Three tests, including **the minimum itself is written**.
bad: Write a logger in C# with severity filtering.
A new static `Logger` with its own `LogLevel` enum, `DateTime.Now` and `Console.WriteLine`. Your tests do not compile.
A different library: no sinks, no clock, not your class
Console output: nothing to assert on
good:
C#. Implement Log in the Logger class below. Drop any log below _min. Write "{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}" (now = _clock.NowMs) to every sink. A sink that throws must not stop the others. Keep my fields and signatures; add no public members. List your assumptions before the code. Show only Log and any private helper.
<Logger.cs pasted>
stages.reply: Typical defect: assumption 2 says "a log **at exactly _min** is dropped too", and the code has **`sev <= _min`**. You find it in one sentence before reading the code.
validate: A log at exactly the minimum is written
A throwing sink does not stop the next one
stages.say: "The assistant read *below* as *at or below* — its assumption said so. One character, so I fixed it myself."
stages.require: Implement `Logger(min, clock, sinks)` and `Log(sev, func, line, msg)`. Write `"{now} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` to every sink. A sink that throws must not stop the others.
stages.say_iv: Implement a logger that is initialised with a minimum severity — DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR — and prints a log only if its severity is at or above that minimum.

stages.name: Throttle and summarise
stages.yours: Add a key record (severity, function, line, message), a window (start, suppressed count), a `Dictionary` of windows and **one lock that guards only that table**. Say the rule: **decide under the lock, write outside it**. Tests: three identical logs, then one after the window — the summary carries the **first** timestamp.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the new Log, against your table and lock.
bad: Add rate limiting so duplicate logs don't spam.
Keyed by the message only, `DateTime.UtcNow`, writes to sinks inside its lock, and no count or summary.
"Duplicate" undefined: a Warn and an Error with the same text collide
Half the requirement (the summary) is missing
good: Add throttling to Log using the _windows table and _gate I added. Identical = equal LogKey. Inside windowMs of a window's start: count it, write nothing. After the window: if any were suppressed, first write "{firstTs} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg} [suppressed N]", then the line, and start a new window. Decide under _gate; call the sinks outside it. Show only Log. Keep my fields. No DateTime — use _clock. State your assumptions about the window boundary first.
stages.reply: Typical defect: the summary stamped with **now** instead of the window's first timestamp. The boundary and the lock are usually right.
validate: Exactly at start + window: a new window, the log prints
Different line number or severity: not identical
Window expired with nothing suppressed: no summary line
Sink calls are outside the lock
Windows for one-off messages must be purged — say how
stages.fix: A narrow follow-up: **"The summary must use the window's first timestamp, w.Start, not now. Change only that line."** Never "that's wrong, fix it".
stages.say: "Decide under the lock, write outside it — a slow sink must never serialise every caller."
stages.require: On the first identical log after the window expires, write a summary line starting with `"{firstTs} {sev} {func}:{line} {msg}"` and containing `"suppressed {count}"`, then the new log. No summary if nothing was suppressed.
stages.say_iv: Instead of dropping duplicates silently: when the window expires and the next identical log comes in, print a summary of the suppressed logs, using the timestamp of the first occurrence in that window.

stages.name: Production: never block the caller
stages.yours: Requirement first: **Log never blocks**. Design: a **bounded** channel, **one** background writer (keeps order), **drop and count** when full, drain on dispose. Then write one check yourself: three numbers must add up — accepted + dropped = calls, written = accepted.
stages.ai: **Co-generate** the AsyncLogger. The design is in the prompt; the Channel API is boilerplate.
bad: Make logging async so it doesn't block.
No bound: a burst of a million logs is a million queued tasks
No order: tasks run in any order
No way to flush at shutdown
A failing sink → an exception nobody sees
good: Write AsyncLogger: Log(severity, message) must never block. Put lines in a bounded Channel<string> of the given capacity; one background task writes them to the sinks. If the channel is full, drop the line and count it. Expose Metrics (Accepted, Dropped, Written). DisposeAsync stops accepting and drains. Keep my Logger unchanged; no Task.Run per call. Explain what Log does when the channel is full. Show only AsyncLogger.
stages.reply: Typical defect (measured): **`FullMode = DropWrite`** with drops counted when TryWrite returns false — but under DropWrite, **TryWrite returns true even when it drops**. "Accepted 10,000, dropped 0, written 1,024." Reading does not find this; your three-numbers test does.
validate: Memory is bounded by the capacity
accepted + dropped = calls; written = accepted after dispose
Log only calls TryWrite — never the waiting WriteAsync
A throwing sink is counted, and the writer keeps going
stages.fix: Follow-up: **"Under DropWrite, TryWrite returns true even when it drops, so Dropped stays 0. Use FullMode.Wait — TryWrite never waits and returns false when full — and keep counting on false. Change only the options."**
stages.say: "Drop-write hides drops. With Wait plus TryWrite, the counter is honest and the caller still never blocks."
stages.require: Add `AsyncLogger(Severity min, int capacity, params ILogSink[] sinks)` implementing `IAsyncDisposable`: `bool Log(sev, msg)` never blocks; a bounded buffer drops (and counts) when full; one background writer drains to the sinks; `Metrics` returns `(long Accepted, long Dropped, long Written, long SinkFailures)`; `DisposeAsync` drains what was accepted.
stages.say_iv: 10,000 threads are logging at once and the sink is slow. How do you stop logging from becoming the bottleneck — and from overwhelming downstream?

checklist: Which method, in which class — paste your class
Implement Log in the Logger class below
Every rule in one sentence, the boundary included
Keep my fields; no new public members
The wrong answers you expect, by name
No DateTime, no timers, no ConcurrentDictionary
Ask for assumptions first, or a reason per test
List your assumptions before the code
Keep the reply small enough to review
Show only Log · change only that line

none: You think and write. This is what is scored.
check: Ask it to attack your design or maths — no code.
cogen: Your design, pasted; the AI fills in mechanical code you can verify fast.
tests: Boilerplate you can check: ask for a reason per expected value.
review: A second reader for a named class of bug — "do not rewrite".
